questions.stem: How does Frankenstein begin?
options: With Elizabeth's letters to Victor describing the murder of his brother
With letters from Robert Walton, an Arctic explorer, to his sister in England
With Victor Frankenstein's diary entries written in his laboratory at Ingolstadt
With the creature telling his story to a blind old man in a cottage
questions.explanation: The novel opens with Walton's letters to his sister, Mrs Saville. Walton's ship is trapped in the ice, and he rescues a dying stranger, Victor, who then tells him his story.

questions.stem: Where does Victor bring the creature to life?
options: In his father's house in Geneva, beside the lake
In a stone hut on one of the remotest Orkney islands
In a cabin aboard Walton's ship in the Arctic
In his rooms at the university town of Ingolstadt
questions.explanation: Victor builds the creature while studying at Ingolstadt, cut off from his family and friends. He later begins a second creature in the Orkneys but destroys it.

questions.stem: How does Victor react when the creature first opens its eyes?
options: He is calm and writes to his father to describe what he has achieved
He is horrified by its appearance and runs from the room, abandoning it
He is delighted and teaches it to speak before showing it to Clerval
He is frightened and tries to destroy it at once before it can leave the room
questions.explanation: After nearly two years of work, Victor is disgusted by what he has made and flees. His abandonment of the creature at the moment of its 'birth' is central to the novel's question of responsibility.

questions.stem: Who is the creature's first victim?
options: Henry Clerval, Victor's closest friend, killed in Ireland
Elizabeth, Victor's bride, killed on their wedding night
Justine Moritz, the Frankensteins' servant, killed in prison
William, Victor's young brother, killed near Geneva
questions.explanation: The creature meets William by chance, learns he is a Frankenstein and kills him. It is the first of the deaths that strike at Victor through the people he loves.

questions.stem: Why is Justine Moritz executed?
options: She is convicted of William's murder after Victor tells the court he saw her with the boy that night
She is convicted of stealing from the Frankensteins after Elizabeth's jewels are found in her room
She is convicted of helping the creature escape after she is seen with him in the woods near Geneva
She is convicted of William's murder after the creature hides William's miniature portrait in her dress
questions.explanation: The creature plants the portrait William was wearing on the sleeping Justine. Victor knows she is innocent but stays silent, fearing he will be thought mad, so his guilt grows.

questions.stem: Where do Victor and the creature meet, and the creature tells his story?
options: On the glacier near Montanvert, in the Alps below Mont Blanc
In the anatomy theatre of the university at Ingolstadt
On the deck of Walton's ship, trapped in the Arctic ice
In the prison cell in Ireland where Victor is held
questions.explanation: Victor climbs Montanvert alone and the creature approaches him across the sea of ice. In a hut on the mountain the creature tells his story, which forms the centre of the novel.

questions.stem: How does the creature learn to speak and read?
options: By secretly watching the De Lacey family through a gap in the wall of their cottage
By listening to Victor's lectures from outside the windows of the university
By studying the books he finds in Victor's abandoned laboratory at Ingolstadt
By living with Walton's sailors on the ship before Victor is rescued from the ice
questions.explanation: Hiding in a hovel beside the cottage, the creature learns language as Felix teaches it to Safie. He also learns about history, injustice and family love, which makes his own loneliness clearer.

questions.stem: What happens when the creature finally reveals himself to the De Lacey family?
options: Felix offers him work, but the blind father orders him from the house
The blind father listens kindly, but Felix returns and beats him away
The whole family welcomes him, but Victor arrives and drives him off
Safie teaches him to read, but Agatha betrays him to the angry villagers
questions.explanation: Old De Lacey cannot see him and treats him with sympathy. When the others return, Felix attacks him with a stick. This rejection by the people he loves turns the creature toward revenge.

questions.stem: What does the creature ask Victor to make, and what does he promise in return?
options: A place in Victor's household; he promises to serve the Frankenstein family faithfully
A female companion; he promises to go with her to the wilds of South America
A new body; he promises to stop killing once he looks like other men
Victor's friendship; he promises to protect the Frankenstein family
questions.explanation: The creature argues that loneliness has made him wicked. He promises that he and his companion will live far from people and harm no one.

questions.stem: Why does Victor tear apart the female creature he is building in the Orkneys?
options: He fears the two creatures could breed and threaten the whole human race
He realises he has run out of the materials needed to finish the work
He learns that the creature has already killed Elizabeth in Geneva
He has promised Elizabeth that he will give up science before their wedding
questions.explanation: Victor imagines that the female might refuse the bargain or that the pair might have children. The creature watches him destroy her and swears revenge.

questions.stem: What happens to Henry Clerval?
options: He dies of a fever in Ingolstadt while nursing Victor through his illness
He drowns in Lake Geneva while sailing with Victor and Elizabeth
He is executed after confessing to a murder in order to protect Victor
The creature strangles him, and Victor is arrested for the murder in Ireland
questions.explanation: After Victor destroys the female, the creature kills Clerval. Victor lands in Ireland, is accused of the murder and falls ill in prison before he is cleared.

questions.stem: What happens on Victor and Elizabeth's wedding night?
options: The creature kills Victor's father as the couple leave for their journey
Victor confesses everything to Elizabeth and she breaks off the marriage
The creature appears at the window and Victor shoots him dead
The creature kills Elizabeth while Victor is searching the inn for him
questions.explanation: Victor believes the threat 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night' is aimed at himself. While he searches for the creature, Elizabeth is killed. Victor's father dies soon after.

questions.stem: How does the novel end?
options: Victor kills the creature on the ice and returns to Geneva with Walton
Walton captures the creature and brings him back to England in chains
The creature dies on Walton's ship and Victor leaves to explore the Pole
Victor dies on Walton's ship and the creature vows to destroy himself in the Arctic
questions.explanation: Walton agrees to turn back, and Victor dies soon after. The creature mourns over his maker, says he will burn himself on a funeral pile, and disappears into the darkness.

questions.stem: Why is Frankenstein often described as a frame narrative with nested stories?
options: Elizabeth's letters contain Clerval's story, which in turn contains Walton's
Walton's letters contain Victor's story, which in turn contains the creature's
Victor's diary contains Walton's letters, which in turn contain Elizabeth's
The creature's story contains Victor's, which in turn contains Walton's letters
questions.explanation: The three narratives sit inside each other like boxes, with the creature's voice at the centre. Each narrator shapes what we hear, so readers must judge how far to trust each account.

questions.stem: How is Robert Walton a parallel to Victor?
options: He also abandons his family in Geneva to study at a German university
He is also driven by ambition to discover what no one has achieved
He is also a scientist who creates new life in his ship's laboratory
He also loses a brother and a friend to a monster he has made
questions.explanation: Walton wants glory from reaching the Pole, just as Victor wanted it from creating life. Victor's story is a warning to him, and Walton's choice to turn back is the path Victor did not take.

questions.stem: Henry Clerval is best described as:
options: Victor's rival at Ingolstadt, who tries to steal the secret of creating life
Victor's professor of chemistry, who first inspires him to study modern science
Victor's younger brother, who joins him in England to help build the female
Victor's loyal friend, who loves literature and nature and nurses him back to health
questions.explanation: Clerval is warm, sociable and delighted by the world. He acts as a foil to Victor's isolated obsession, which makes his death especially painful.

questions.stem: Which books does the creature find and learn from?
options: The Sorrows of Werter, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Hamlet
Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives and The Sorrows of Werter
Paradise Lost, the works of Cornelius Agrippa and the Bible
Plutarch's Lives, a history of Geneva and Victor's own journal
questions.explanation: The three books teach him about feeling, virtue and history. Paradise Lost matters most: he compares himself to Adam and to Satan. He also reads Victor's journal, found in clothes he took from the laboratory.

questions.stem: How does the novel challenge the label 'monster' for the creature?
options: He is shown to be handsome, but everyone around him is too afraid to look at him
He is innocent of William's death, which Justine actually commits
He begins gentle and kind, and turns violent only after repeated rejection
He is driven to kill by the ambition he inherits from Victor
questions.explanation: The creature saves a drowning girl and secretly gathers wood for the De Laceys. He is attacked for his appearance each time, so the novel invites us to ask who the real monster is.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Victor's failure as a creator?
options: He gives his creation no ability to speak, so it cannot explain itself
He abandons his creation and refuses responsibility until it is too late
He makes his creation too weak to survive without his constant care
He tells everyone about his creation, so people hunt it down from the very start
questions.explanation: Victor flees his creation, stays silent at Justine's trial and never tells anyone the truth in time. The novel suggests that his neglect, not just his ambition, causes the deaths that follow.

questions.stem: In what circumstances did Mary Shelley begin Frankenstein, according to her 1831 introduction?
options: A ghost-story contest with Lord Byron and Percy Shelley near Geneva in 1816
A writing prize offered by a London magazine for the best Gothic novel in 1816
A bet with her father, William Godwin, about whether she could write a novel
A request from her publisher for a sequel to her mother's famous Gothic tale
questions.explanation: In the cold, wet summer of 1816, Byron proposed that each of the group write a ghost story. Mary's idea came to her in a waking dream of a 'pale student' kneeling beside the thing he had made.

questions.stem: Why is the novel subtitled 'The Modern Prometheus'?
options: In Greek myth Prometheus is a monster made of river clay who destroys his maker
In Greek myth Prometheus flies too close to the sun and falls into the sea
In Greek myth Prometheus builds a labyrinth to imprison a dangerous beast
In Greek myth Prometheus defies the gods to give humans fire, and is punished
questions.explanation: Like Prometheus, Victor oversteps the limits set for humans by seizing a godlike power, and he suffers for it. In some versions Prometheus also shaped humans from clay.

questions.stem: Which scientific idea of Shelley's time is most linked to Victor's work?
options: Evolution by natural selection, as set out by Charles Darwin
Vaccination, the use of cowpox to protect people from smallpox
Atomic theory, the idea that all matter is made of atoms
Galvanism, the use of electricity to make dead muscles move
questions.explanation: Experiments in Shelley's time showed that electric current could make dead animals' limbs twitch. Her 1831 introduction says galvanism had suggested a corpse might be brought back to life. Darwin's theory came decades later.

questions.stem: Which feature of the novel most clearly reflects the Romantic movement?
options: A trust in calm reason and social order over feeling and imagination
A focus on crowded industrial cities and factory life
Satire of fashionable society through witty dialogue
Wild, sublime landscapes such as the Alps that stir powerful emotion
questions.explanation: Romantic writers valued feeling, imagination and the awe of nature. Victor seeks comfort in the mountains, and the meeting on the glacier is set against the sublime scenery around Mont Blanc.

questions.stem: Mary Shelley's mother was Mary Wollstonecraft. Why is this often noted in readings of the novel?
options: Wollstonecraft wrote Gothic novels, and she helped her daughter to plan the story
Wollstonecraft was a philosopher of science, and she inspired Victor's studies
Wollstonecraft argued for women's rights, and the novel's women are mostly passive victims
Wollstonecraft argued for women's rights, and the novel's women lead its action
questions.explanation: Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. Critics note that Elizabeth, Justine and Caroline are good but have little power, and that Victor tries to create life without a woman.

questions.stem: Which theme is most central to Frankenstein?
options: The triumph of scientific progress over religious superstition
The power of revenge to restore justice to those who have been wronged
The power of nature to heal the guilt and grief of the mind
The dangers of ambition and of knowledge pursued without responsibility
questions.explanation: Victor's hunger for discovery cuts him off from family and leads to disaster. He tells Walton his story as a warning against the same kind of ambition.

questions.stem: How does the novel explore nature versus nurture?
options: The De Laceys argue that their kindness could have made the creature good
The creature argues that cruelty and rejection, not his nature, made him evil
The creature argues that he was evil from birth, whatever anyone did for him
Victor argues that the creature's evil comes from the corpses used to make him
questions.explanation: The creature insists he was 'benevolent and good' until misery made him a fiend. The novel asks whether he was born a monster or was made one by the way he was treated.

questions.stem: How does isolation link Victor, Walton and the creature?
options: All three find lasting friendship that ends their loneliness
All three suffer from loneliness, though the creature is the most completely alone
All three choose solitude as the price of pursuing great knowledge
All three are cut off from their families by the murders that the creature commits
questions.explanation: Walton longs for a friend, Victor isolates himself in his work, and the creature is rejected by everyone. The creature's request for a companion makes the need for connection the novel's moral centre.

questions.stem: What does the novel suggest about how people judge by appearance?
options: That appearance is a reliable guide to a person's true moral character
That children are free of prejudice until adults teach it to them
That the creature's ugliness is exaggerated by Victor's guilty and fevered imagination
That fear of difference leads people to reject the creature before he can speak
questions.explanation: Only the blind De Lacey treats the creature fairly, because he cannot see him. Everyone else reacts with horror, so the novel exposes prejudice based on how someone looks.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of letting the creature tell his own story in the middle of the novel?
options: It shifts the story's focus away from moral questions to adventure
It lets readers hear his side and sympathise with him, after seeing him through Victor's eyes
It confirms Victor's view of the creature as a fiend from the start
It distances readers from the creature by presenting him coldly
questions.explanation: Until then we know the creature only through Victor's horrified descriptions. His eloquent, moving account changes our view and makes the novel's moral questions harder to answer.

questions.stem: How does the novel use allusions to Milton's Paradise Lost?
options: Elizabeth compares herself to Eve, tempting Victor to seek forbidden knowledge
The creature compares himself to Adam and to Satan, rejected by his creator
Victor compares himself to Noah, saving his family from a coming flood
Walton compares himself to Moses, leading his crew to a promised land
questions.explanation: Like Adam the creature is made and alone; like Satan he feels cast out and turns to revenge. The allusion frames the novel as a story about a creator and the being he abandons.

questions.stem: The creation scene opens on 'a dreary night of November' with rain beating on the window. What technique is this?
options: Dramatic irony, where the creature knows more than Victor at this point
Personification, where the creature is described as if it were part of the weather
Flashback, where Victor remembers a stormy night from his childhood
Pathetic fallacy, where the weather reflects mood and foreshadows disaster
questions.explanation: The gloomy setting matches Victor's anxiety and the horror that follows. Storms and lightning recur at key moments, a typical Gothic device.

questions.stem: Victor quotes Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner as he flees through Ingolstadt after the creation. What does the allusion suggest?
options: Like the mariner, Victor plans to sail to the Arctic to find the creature
Like the mariner, Victor has been rescued from the sea by a kindly stranger
Like the mariner, Victor is blamed by a ship's crew for their bad luck
Like the mariner, Victor has committed a wrong against nature and is haunted by it
questions.explanation: The lines describe a man afraid to look back because 'a frightful fiend' follows him. In the 1831 text Walton also mentions the poem, linking two men who push past natural limits.

questions.stem: Who says 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend'?
options: Victor, confessing his crimes to Walton on the ship
Walton, writing to his sister about the creature
Felix, explaining why he attacked the stranger
The creature, pleading with Victor on the glacier
questions.explanation: The creature says this when he first confronts Victor. It sums up his argument that suffering and rejection, not his nature, have made him violent.

questions.stem: Victor tells Walton, 'Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge'. What does this show?
options: His story is meant as a warning against Walton's own reckless ambition
His wish to teach Walton the scientific method he used to create life
His belief that Walton is far too ignorant to understand natural science
His regret that he did not share his discovery with other scientists
questions.explanation: Victor sees his own ambition in Walton. The line turns the whole novel into a cautionary tale, though Victor still refuses to reveal how he made the creature.

questions.stem: When the creature says 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night', what does Victor misunderstand?
options: He thinks the creature will attend as a guest and ask to be forgiven
He thinks the creature means Clerval's wedding, so he warns his friend
He thinks it is an empty threat, so he does not bother to arm himself at all
He thinks he will be the victim, but the creature means to kill Elizabeth
questions.explanation: The creature says it after Victor destroys the female companion. Victor's self-centred reading of the threat leaves Elizabeth unprotected.

questions.stem: The creature tells Victor, 'I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel'. What does he mean?
options: He should have been the first of a new race, but has decided to rule over men
He should have been given a wife like Adam, but now prefers to remain alone
He should have been an angel who serves God, but has chosen to become human
He should have been loved like the first man, but has been cast out like Satan
questions.explanation: The allusion to Paradise Lost casts Victor as a careless God. The creature feels driven from joy 'for no misdeed', which makes his anger seem a response to injustice.

questions.stem: After the creation, Victor says 'the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart'. What does this reveal?
options: His fear that Clerval will discover the creature and tell his father
His sorrow that his mother did not live long enough to see his success
His ambition blinded him, and he rejects his creation the moment it lives
His relief that the experiment failed and the creature did not wake
questions.explanation: Victor worked for two years imagining a beautiful achievement. The sudden shift to disgust shows how little he considered the being he was making, and starts its abandonment.

questions.stem: Who writes 'I have no friend, Margaret'?
options: Elizabeth, in a letter to Victor after Justine's death
Clerval, in a letter to his mother from Oxford
Walton, in a letter to his sister before he meets Victor
Victor, in a letter to Elizabeth while he is in Ingolstadt
questions.explanation: Walton's loneliness introduces the theme of isolation before we meet Victor or the creature. It also explains why he grows so attached to the dying stranger.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the task 'Analyse how Shelley positions readers to view the creature'?
options: Shelley gives the creature his own eloquent voice, positioning readers to see him as a victim of rejection
In Frankenstein the creature is made by Victor at Ingolstadt and later kills several of Victor's family
This essay will analyse the creature in Frankenstein, a novel written by Mary Shelley in 1818
Frankenstein is a famous Gothic novel which many people know from its film versions
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence names the writer's choice and the effect on readers. The others retell the plot, announce the essay or state facts without an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The creature saves a girl from drowning but a man shoots him.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Add the name of the river and the season in which the rescue takes place
List the other good deeds the creature does, such as gathering wood
Describe what the creature does next, one event at a time
Explain how the scene shows kindness repaid with violence, building sympathy for him
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence shows and why it matters. Linking the rescue to the theme of prejudice turns a plot detail into an argument.
